newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stock fever grips Germany as Telekom offer nears.
newsitem.headline: Stock fever grips Germany as Telekom offer nears.

text.p: Stock market fever gripped Germany on Friday ahead of next week's $12 billion listing of Deutsche Telekom, the phone giant about to launch Europe's largest-ever share offering.

Anticipation of huge volumes when Telekom shares trade on stock exchanges in Germany, New York and Tokyo buoyed already bullish sentiment in Frankfurt which has driven the DAX index of 30 blue-chip stocks into record territory.

Banking officials said that with around 3.6 billion Telekom shares ordered by the close of the subscription period on Thursday, the issue would be oversubscribed six times and the price would be driven up.

The main underwriting banks -- Deutsche Bank AG, Dresdner Bank AG and Goldman Sachs -- will announce the share price and allocation details on Sunday. Shares begin trading in Germany and the United States on Monday and a day later in Japan.
Deutsche Telekom shares traded in the grey market on Friday around 33.50 marks ($22.22), some 11.66 percent above the top of the expected range of 25-30 marks set last month.

"The large interest, especially from private investors, will guarantuee a price of nearly 30 marks," Florian Weber, share trader with Duesseldorf brokers Schnigge & Partner, told Reuters Financial Television.

One of the world's largest initial public offerings of stock, Telekom will float up to 690 million shares with a face value of five marks each, just over 26 percent of its capital, on international stock exchanges. Another 30 million shares will be sold to Telekom employees.

The issue has sparked the imagination of millions of ordinary Germans, many first time investors, who have tossed caution to the wind and cracked open piggy banks and bet their savings to make a fortune on the stock market.

Telekom offered individual investors discounts of 50 pfennigs a share, dividends of 60 pfennigs this year and around 1.20 marks next year, as well as a bonus share for every ten shares held for at least three years.
The German government and the financial community are hoping that the enormous interest on the part of amateur investors will be the catalyst needed to promote broad-based investment in shares.

The short-term success of Telekom's share offering is nearly certain because the company's five percent weighting in the DAX index, making it one of the largest DAX shares, means funds will have to include it in their German portfolios.
But Telekom must convince investors in the long-term that by cutting its debt mountain of over 100 billion marks and turning huge investments of the past few years into profits.

"I think it's a good long-term investment. There are a number of positive surprises from some areas of the business that will add to profits over time," said Talal Shakerchi, head of European equities at British fund Old Mutual Hook.
Germany's leading banks called in hundreds of employees to work on Sunday to count orders and book share purchases.
Commerzbank, Germany's third-largest commercial bank, will have 140 employees in the office on Sunday and Deutsche Bank, Germany's biggest bank, plans to have 100 people at work.
While the Frankfurt stock exchange has dealt with up to 120,000 share orders on high-volume days, its computers are set to handle up to 600,000 transactions next Monday.
Scaffolding clung to the facade of the stock exchange on Friday afternoon as the bourse made final preparations for Monday's spectacle.
InfoRadio, a Berlin business radio programme, said it would announce regular updates every thirty minutes on the development of Telekom's share price on Monday.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing, said German investment in new Telekom shares could even affect money supply growth, a key inflation indicator.
"(The investment) adds up to sums that could impact the data and may have an expansive impact on the data," Issing told reporters, adding that the effect would be short-term.
($ = 1.506 German Marks)
